Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 37, verse 6–10:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven﴾, meaning the one that is nearest to the earth, the lowest of the heavens, ﴿with an adornment of the stars﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "bi-zinati al-kawakibi" with the noun in the genitive construct (idafa), meaning: with their beauty and their light. Hamza and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "bi-zinatin" with tanwin and with the genitive "al-kawakibi," making "al-kawakibi" a substitute (badal) for "zinah," because it is that (adornment), just as you say: "marartu bi-Abi 'Abd Allah Zaydin" (I passed by Abu 'Abd Allah, Zayd). The meaning is: We adorned the nearest heaven with the stars. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read "bi-zinatin" with tanwin and with the accusative "al-kawakiba," and the meaning is: We adorned the nearest heaven by adorning the stars in it when We set them in their stations and made them possessors of light. Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that "al-kawakibi" in the accusative be a substitute for "bi-zinatin," because "bi-zinatin" is in a position of accusative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh al-Qari', Abu Nahik, Abu Husayn al-Asadi and others read "bi-zinatin" with tanwin and "al-kawakibu" with a nominative (raf') ending. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: We adorned the nearest heaven in that the stars adorned it, and in that the stars adorned themselves. ﴿And as protection﴾, meaning: and We protected it, a protection. As for al-marid (the rebellious), it is the defiant one, and we have explained this in His saying: ﴿a rebellious devil﴾ [an-Nisa': 117].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They cannot listen﴾. Al-Farra' said: "La" here is like His saying: ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals. They will not believe in it﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 200–201]; and in "la" on this meaning, the jussive (jazm) is appropriate, for the Arabs say: "I tied the horse, it does not break loose" (rabatat al-faras la yanfalitu). Others said: so that they do not listen to the Highest Assembly, who are the angels in the heaven. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read "la yassamma'una" with the sin doubled, and its original form is "yatasamma'una," so the ta' was assimilated into the sin. He said "to the Highest Assembly" because the Arabs say: "I heard so-and-so," "I heard from so-and-so," and "to so-and-so."

﴿And they are pelted from every side﴾ with meteors, ﴿repulsion﴾. Qatadah said: meaning, a pelting with meteors. Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning, driving away; it is said: "dahartuhu dahran wa duhuran," meaning, I pushed him away. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Raja', Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Dahhak, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "duhuran" with a fatha on the dal.

Regarding "al-wasib" there are two views.

One: it is the perpetual, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: it is the painful, said by Abu Salih and al-Suddi.

Regarding the time of this punishment there are two views. One: it is in the Hereafter. The second: it is in this world, so they are struck by the meteors and are stunned until the first blast in the Trumpet.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except one who snatches away a snatch﴾. Ibn as-Sumayfa' read "khatifa" with a fatha on the kha' and a kasra on the ta' and its doubling. Abu Raja' and al-Jahdari read it with a kasra on both the kha' and the ta' and without doubling. Al-Zajjaj said: "khatifa" and "khatafa," with the ta' vowelled with kasra or fatha, are both used; it is said: "khataftu akhtafu" and "khatiftu akhtifu," when you take something swiftly. "Illa man khataifa" may be read with a fatha on the kha' and doubling of the ta', and "khifata" may be read with a kasra on the kha' and a fatha on the ta'; the meaning is: "ikhtatafa," the ta' was assimilated into the ta', and the alif dropped because of the vowel of the kha'. Whoever reads the kha' with a fatha places on it the fatha of the ta' that was in "ikhtatafa"; whoever reads the kha' with a kasra does so because of its sukun and the sukun of the ta'. As for whoever reports "khataifa" with a kasra on the kha' and the ta', there is no basis for it except a very weak one, namely that the ta' takes the kasra of the kha' by assimilation. The exegetes said: the meaning is: except one who snatches a word from the speech of the angels stealthily, ﴿so there follows him﴾, meaning: he is overtaken by ﴿a piercing flame﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning, a shining star. It is said: "athqib naraka," meaning, light it, and ath-thuqub is that with which fire is kindled.

Hamza and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "bi-zinatin" with tanwin and with the genitive "al-kawakibi," making "al-kawakibi" a substitute (badal) for "zinah," because it is that (adornment), just as you say: "marartu bi-Abi 'Abd Allah Zaydin" (I passed by Abu 'Abd Allah, Zayd). The meaning is: We adorned the nearest heaven with the stars. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read "bi-zinatin" with tanwin and with the accusative "al-kawakiba," and the meaning is: We adorned the nearest heaven by adorning the stars in it when We set them in their stations and made them possessors of light. Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that "al-kawakibi" in the accusative be a substitute for "bi-zinatin," because "bi-zinatin" is in a position of accusative. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh al-Qari', Abu Nahik, Abu Husayn al-Asadi and others read "bi-zinatin" with tanwin and "al-kawakibu" with a nominative (raf') ending. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: We adorned the nearest heaven in that the stars adorned it, and in that the stars adorned themselves. ﴿And as protection﴾, meaning: and We protected it, a protection. As for al-marid (the rebellious), it is the defiant one, and we have explained this in His saying: ﴿a rebellious devil﴾ [an-Nisa': 117].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They cannot listen﴾. Al-Farra' said: "La" here is like His saying: ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals. They will not believe in it﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 200–201]; and in "la" on this meaning, the jussive (jazm) is appropriate, for the Arabs say: "I tied the horse, it does not break loose" (rabatat al-faras la yanfalitu). Others said: so that they do not listen to the Highest Assembly, who are the angels in the heaven. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read "la yassamma'una" with the sin doubled, and its original form is "yatasamma'una," so the ta' was assimilated into the sin. He said "to the Highest Assembly" because the Arabs say: "I heard so-and-so," "I heard from so-and-so," and "to so-and-so."

﴿And they are pelted from every side﴾ with meteors, ﴿repulsion﴾. Qatadah said: meaning, a pelting with meteors. Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning, driving away; it is said: "dahartuhu dahran wa duhuran," meaning, I pushed him away. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Raja', Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Dahhak, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "duhuran" with a fatha on the dal.

Regarding "al-wasib" there are two views.

One: it is the perpetual, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: it is the painful, said by Abu Salih and al-Suddi.

Regarding the time of this punishment there are two views. One: it is in the Hereafter. The second: it is in this world, so they are struck by the meteors and are stunned until the first blast in the Trumpet.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except one who snatches away a snatch﴾. Ibn as-Sumayfa' read "khatifa" with a fatha on the kha' and a kasra on the ta' and its doubling. Abu Raja' and al-Jahdari read it with a kasra on both the kha' and the ta' and without doubling. Al-Zajjaj said: "khatifa" and "khatafa," with the ta' vowelled with kasra or fatha, are both used; it is said: "khataftu akhtafu" and "khatiftu akhtifu," when you take something swiftly. "Illa man khataifa" may be read with a fatha on the kha' and doubling of the ta', and "khifata" may be read with a kasra on the kha' and a fatha on the ta'; the meaning is: "ikhtatafa," the ta' was assimilated into the ta', and the alif dropped because of the vowel of the kha'. Whoever reads the kha' with a fatha places on it the fatha of the ta' that was in "ikhtatafa"; whoever reads the kha' with a kasra does so because of its sukun and the sukun of the ta'. As for whoever reports "khataifa" with a kasra on the kha' and the ta', there is no basis for it except a very weak one, namely that the ta' takes the kasra of the kha' by assimilation. The exegetes said: the meaning is: except one who snatches a word from the speech of the angels stealthily, ﴿so there follows him﴾, meaning: he is overtaken by ﴿a piercing flame﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning, a shining star. It is said: "athqib naraka," meaning, light it, and ath-thuqub is that with which fire is kindled.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 37, verses 11–26:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So ask them﴾, meaning: ask them a question of rebuke (*taqrir*), ﴿Are they stronger in creation﴾, meaning: more firm in their workmanship, ﴿or those We have created?﴾ On this there are two opinions.

One: the meaning is, "Or those whose creation We have counted, from among the angels, the devils, the heavens and the earth." This is the view of Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari).

The second: "Or those We created before them from the earlier nations. The meaning is that they are not stronger than those, and We destroyed them for their denial. So what would make these people safe?"

Then He mentioned the creation of mankind, saying: ﴿Indeed, We created them from sticky clay﴾. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba said: that is, adhering and clinging. The letter *ba'* (ب) is substituted for *mim* (م) because their points of articulation are close. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is pure, good, sticky clay. Others said: it is clay from which water seeps away, leaving its moisture within, so that it clings to the hand like wax. This is an informing that the origin of their creation and the creation of those before them is the same; so whoever is able to destroy the strong is able to destroy the weak.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But you marvel﴾. The word *bal* (بَلْ) means leaving aside the first speech and taking up another speech, as if He had said: "Leave aside, O Muhammad, what has passed."

There are two recitations of *'ajibta* (عَجِبْتَ). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited *bal 'ajibta* (بَلْ عَجِبْتَ) with an open *ta'* (فتح التاء). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, among others, recited *bal 'ajibtu* (بَلْ عَجِبْتُ) with a *damma* on the *ta'* (ضم التاء), and al-Farra' preferred this reading.

Whoever reads with the open *ta'* means: "Rather, you marvel, O Muhammad," ﴿and they mock﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: you marvel at them, and they mock you. Regarding what he marvelled at, there are two opinions: one, at the disbelievers who did not believe in the Qur'an; the other, at their disbelief in the Resurrection.

Whoever reads with the *damma* intends to inform that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, (p-٥٠) marvelled. Al-Farra' said: this is the recitation of 'Ali, 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas, and it is more beloved to me. Some people rejected this recitation, among them Shurayh al-Qadi, who said: "Allah does not marvel; only one who does not know marvels." Al-Zajjaj said: rejecting this recitation is an error, because the marvelling of Allah differs from the marvelling of human beings. This is like His saying: ﴿And Allah plans﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] and His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 79]. The basic meaning of *'ajab* in the language is that when a person sees something he denies and which is rare, he says, "I have marvelled at such-and-such." Likewise, when human beings do what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, denies, it is permissible to say "I marvelled," though Allah knows the thing before it occurs. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is "I requited them for their marvelling at the truth." So He named the requital for a thing by the name of the thing for which the requital is given, and named His act "marvelling," though it is not marvelling in reality, because one who marvels is astonished and bewildered, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above that. Likewise, the magnification of reward is called marvelling, because one marvels at a thing only when it is at its extreme. The Arabs name an action by the name of another action when it approximates it in some respect, even if it differs from it in most of its meanings. 'Adi said:

*"Then they became a plaything of time,*
*And thus time destroys men."*

So he made time's destruction and corruption a plaything. Ibn Jarir said: whoever reads with the *damma* on the *ta'*, the meaning is: "Rather, their taking partners for Me and their denial of My revelation has become great and momentous in My sight." Others said: the attribution of marvelling to Allah is of two kinds: one in the sense of denial and censure, as in this verse; the other in the sense of approval and informing of complete satisfaction, as in His saying, peace be upon him: «"Your Lord marvels at a young man who has no youthful folly."»

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember﴾, meaning: when they are admonished with the Qur'an, they do not take heed and do not accept admonition. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Mutawakkil, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Abu 'Imran recited *dhakkarū* (ذَكَّرُوا) with the *kaf* (الكاف) lightened.

﴿And when they see a sign﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning the splitting of the moon. ﴿They mock﴾ (*yastaskhirun* يَسْتَسْخِرُونَ). Abu 'Ubayda said: *yastaskhirun* and *yaskharun* (يَسْخَرُونَ) are the same. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said *sakhira* and *istaskhara*, just as it is said *qarra* and *istaqarra* (settled), and *'ajiba* and *ista'jaba* (marvelled). It is also possible that they asked others among the polytheists to mock the Messenger of Allah, just as one says *ista'tabtuhu* (I asked him to reproach), *istawhabtuhu* (I asked him for a gift), and *ista'faytuhu* (I asked him to pardon), meaning: I asked him for these things.

﴿And they say: "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾, meaning by "this" the splitting of the moon. That is, it is manifest to whoever reflects on it that it is magic.

﴿When we have died﴾. The explanation of this verse has already passed [Maryam: 66].

﴿And our forefathers?﴾ This interrogative *alif* (أ) entered upon the conjunctive particle, as in His saying: ﴿Or did the people of the cities feel secure﴾ [al-A'raf: 98]. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited *aw ābā'unā al-awwalūn* (أَوْ آبَاؤُنَا الأَوَّلُونَ) with the *waw* (و) here and in [al-Waqi'ah: 48] vocalised with sukun (silent).

﴿Say: "Yes"﴾, meaning: yes, you will be resurrected, ﴿and you will be humbled﴾, meaning: abased.

﴿It will be but one blast﴾, meaning: the matter of the Resurrection will be but one cry from Israfil, and it is the blast of resurrection. It was called *zajra* (زَجْرَة, a shout of driving away) because its purpose is to drive. ﴿Then they will be looking﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, they will be made alive and resurrected, seeing and looking. When they witness their resurrection, they will recall the messengers' report about the Resurrection. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾, meaning the Day of Reckoning and Requital. The angels will say: ﴿This is the Day of Judgement﴾, meaning the Day of Decision in which a distinction is made between the good-doer and the wrongdoer. On that day Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to the angels: ﴿Gather﴾, that is, assemble ﴿those who did wrong﴾ from wherever they are. On who these are there are two opinions: one, that they are the polytheists; the other, that it is general to every wrongdoer. On their *azwāj* (أَزْوَاج, companions/spouses) there are four opinions:

One: their likes and their counterparts. This is the view of 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Mujahid and others. It is narrated from 'Umar that he said: "The one who deals in usury will be gathered with the one who deals in usury, the adulterer with the adulterer, and the drinker of wine with the drinker of wine."

The second: their spouses, the polytheist women. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: their followers (*ashyā'*). This is the view of Qatada.

The fourth: their devilish companions who misled them. This is the view of Muqatil.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and what they used to worship﴾ there are three opinions. One: the idols. This is the view of 'Ikrima and Qatada. The second: Iblis alone. This is the view of Muqatil. The third: the devils, as mentioned by al-Mawardi and others.

[His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾, meaning: direct them to its road; the meaning is: take them to it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *hadaytu al-rajul* (I guided the man) when I showed him the way, *hadaytu al-'arusa ila zawjihā* (I conducted the bride to her husband), and *ahdaytu al-hadiyyah* (I presented the gift). When you make the bride like a gift, you say *ahdaytuhā* (I presented her).]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And detain them﴾, meaning: hold them back, ﴿for they are to be questioned﴾. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited *annahum* (أَنَّهُمْ) with an open *hamza* (فتح الهمزة). The commentators said: when they are driven to the Fire they are held back at the Path (*al-sirāt*), because the questioning takes place there. There are six opinions regarding this questioning:

One: they will be questioned about their deeds and statements in this world. Two: about "There is no god but Allah." Both of these are narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Three: about their sins. This is the view of al-Dahhak. Four: the guardians of Hell asked them: ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] and similar. This is the view of Muqatil. Five: they will be asked about what they used to worship. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. Six: their question is His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾, [mentioned by al-Mawardi]. The commentators said: the meaning is, "What is the matter with you that one of you does not help the other as you used to in the world?" This is the answer of Abu Jahl when he said on the Day of Badr: ﴿We are a united body that is victorious﴾ [al-Qamar: 44], so they were told this on that day as a rebuke. Al-Mustaslim means one who submits, the humbled one who is compliant; the meaning is that they are submissive, having no means of escape.

So he made time's destruction and corruption a plaything. Ibn Jarir said: whoever reads with the *damma* on the *ta'*, the meaning is: "Rather, their taking partners for Me and their denial of My revelation has become great and momentous in My sight." Others said: the attribution of marvelling to Allah is of two kinds: one in the sense of denial and censure, as in this verse; the other in the sense of approval and informing of complete satisfaction, as in His saying, peace be upon him: «"Your Lord marvels at a young man who has no youthful folly."»

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember﴾, meaning: when they are admonished with the Qur'an, they do not take heed and do not accept admonition. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Mutawakkil, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Abu 'Imran recited *dhakkarū* (ذَكَّرُوا) with the *kaf* (الكاف) lightened.

﴿And when they see a sign﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning the splitting of the moon. ﴿They mock﴾ (*yastaskhirun* يَسْتَسْخِرُونَ). Abu 'Ubayda said: *yastaskhirun* and *yaskharun* (يَسْخَرُونَ) are the same. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said *sakhira* and *istaskhara*, just as it is said *qarra* and *istaqarra* (settled), and *'ajiba* and *ista'jaba* (marvelled). It is also possible that they asked others among the polytheists to mock the Messenger of Allah, just as one says *ista'tabtuhu* (I asked him to reproach), *istawhabtuhu* (I asked him for a gift), and *ista'faytuhu* (I asked him to pardon), meaning: I asked him for these things.

﴿And they say: "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾, meaning by "this" the splitting of the moon. That is, it is manifest to whoever reflects on it that it is magic.

﴿When we have died﴾. The explanation of this verse has already passed [Maryam: 66].

﴿And our forefathers?﴾ This interrogative *alif* (أ) entered upon the conjunctive particle, as in His saying: ﴿Or did the people of the cities feel secure﴾ [al-A'raf: 98]. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited *aw ābā'unā al-awwalūn* (أَوْ آبَاؤُنَا الأَوَّلُونَ) with the *waw* (و) here and in [al-Waqi'ah: 48] vocalised with sukun (silent).

﴿Say: "Yes"﴾, meaning: yes, you will be resurrected, ﴿and you will be humbled﴾, meaning: abased.

﴿It will be but one blast﴾, meaning: the matter of the Resurrection will be but one cry from Israfil, and it is the blast of resurrection. It was called *zajra* (زَجْرَة, a shout of driving away) because its purpose is to drive. ﴿Then they will be looking﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, they will be made alive and resurrected, seeing and looking. When they witness their resurrection, they will recall the messengers' report about the Resurrection. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾, meaning the Day of Reckoning and Requital. The angels will say: ﴿This is the Day of Judgement﴾, meaning the Day of Decision in which a distinction is made between the good-doer and the wrongdoer. On that day Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to the angels: ﴿Gather﴾, that is, assemble ﴿those who did wrong﴾ from wherever they are. On who these are there are two opinions: one, that they are the polytheists; the other, that it is general to every wrongdoer. On their *azwāj* (أَزْوَاج, companions/spouses) there are four opinions:

One: their likes and their counterparts. This is the view of 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Mujahid and others. It is narrated from 'Umar that he said: "The one who deals in usury will be gathered with the one who deals in usury, the adulterer with the adulterer, and the drinker of wine with the drinker of wine."

The second: their spouses, the polytheist women. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: their followers (*ashyā'*). This is the view of Qatada.

The fourth: their devilish companions who misled them. This is the view of Muqatil.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and what they used to worship﴾ there are three opinions. One: the idols. This is the view of 'Ikrima and Qatada. The second: Iblis alone. This is the view of Muqatil. The third: the devils, as mentioned by al-Mawardi and others.

[His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾, meaning: direct them to its road; the meaning is: take them to it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *hadaytu al-rajul* (I guided the man) when I showed him the way, *hadaytu al-'arusa ila zawjihā* (I conducted the bride to her husband), and *ahdaytu al-hadiyyah* (I presented the gift). When you make the bride like a gift, you say *ahdaytuhā* (I presented her).]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And detain them﴾, meaning: hold them back, ﴿for they are to be questioned﴾. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited *annahum* (أَنَّهُمْ) with an open *hamza* (فتح الهمزة). The commentators said: when they are driven to the Fire they are held back at the Path (*al-sirāt*), because the questioning takes place there. There are six opinions regarding this questioning:

One: they will be questioned about their deeds and statements in this world. Two: about "There is no god but Allah." Both of these are narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Three: about their sins. This is the view of al-Dahhak. Four: the guardians of Hell asked them: ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] and similar. This is the view of Muqatil. Five: they will be asked about what they used to worship. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. Six: their question is His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾, [mentioned by al-Mawardi]. The commentators said: the meaning is, "What is the matter with you that one of you does not help the other as you used to in the world?" This is the answer of Abu Jahl when he said on the Day of Badr: ﴿We are a united body that is victorious﴾ [al-Qamar: 44], so they were told this on that day as a rebuke. Al-Mustaslim means one who submits, the humbled one who is compliant; the meaning is that they are submissive, having no means of escape.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 37, verses 11–26:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So ask them﴾, meaning: ask them a question of rebuke (*taqrir*), ﴿Are they stronger in creation﴾, meaning: more firm in their workmanship, ﴿or those We have created?﴾ On this there are two opinions.

One: the meaning is, "Or those whose creation We have counted, from among the angels, the devils, the heavens and the earth." This is the view of Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari).

The second: "Or those We created before them from the earlier nations. The meaning is that they are not stronger than those, and We destroyed them for their denial. So what would make these people safe?"

Then He mentioned the creation of mankind, saying: ﴿Indeed, We created them from sticky clay﴾. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba said: that is, adhering and clinging. The letter *ba'* (ب) is substituted for *mim* (م) because their points of articulation are close. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is pure, good, sticky clay. Others said: it is clay from which water seeps away, leaving its moisture within, so that it clings to the hand like wax. This is an informing that the origin of their creation and the creation of those before them is the same; so whoever is able to destroy the strong is able to destroy the weak.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But you marvel﴾. The word *bal* (بَلْ) means leaving aside the first speech and taking up another speech, as if He had said: "Leave aside, O Muhammad, what has passed."

There are two recitations of *'ajibta* (عَجِبْتَ). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited *bal 'ajibta* (بَلْ عَجِبْتَ) with an open *ta'* (فتح التاء). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, among others, recited *bal 'ajibtu* (بَلْ عَجِبْتُ) with a *damma* on the *ta'* (ضم التاء), and al-Farra' preferred this reading.

Whoever reads with the open *ta'* means: "Rather, you marvel, O Muhammad," ﴿and they mock﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: you marvel at them, and they mock you. Regarding what he marvelled at, there are two opinions: one, at the disbelievers who did not believe in the Qur'an; the other, at their disbelief in the Resurrection.

Whoever reads with the *damma* intends to inform that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, (p-٥٠) marvelled. Al-Farra' said: this is the recitation of 'Ali, 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas, and it is more beloved to me. Some people rejected this recitation, among them Shurayh al-Qadi, who said: "Allah does not marvel; only one who does not know marvels." Al-Zajjaj said: rejecting this recitation is an error, because the marvelling of Allah differs from the marvelling of human beings. This is like His saying: ﴿And Allah plans﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] and His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 79]. The basic meaning of *'ajab* in the language is that when a person sees something he denies and which is rare, he says, "I have marvelled at such-and-such." Likewise, when human beings do what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, denies, it is permissible to say "I marvelled," though Allah knows the thing before it occurs. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is "I requited them for their marvelling at the truth." So He named the requital for a thing by the name of the thing for which the requital is given, and named His act "marvelling," though it is not marvelling in reality, because one who marvels is astonished and bewildered, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above that. Likewise, the magnification of reward is called marvelling, because one marvels at a thing only when it is at its extreme. The Arabs name an action by the name of another action when it approximates it in some respect, even if it differs from it in most of its meanings. 'Adi said:

*And thus time destroys men."*

And some of them turn to others, questioning one another (﴿وَأقْبَلَ بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾). There are two opinions about who this refers to. The first: the humans turn to the devils. The second: the followers turn to their leaders. ﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ means they question one another in rebuke, reproach and blame. The followers say to the leaders: "Why did you deceive us?" And the leaders say: "Why did you accept from us?" This is the meaning of His words: ﴿قالُوا﴾, meaning the followers say to those who were followed: ﴿إنَّكم كُنْتُمْ تَأْتُونَنا عَنِ اليَمِينِ﴾ ("You used to come to us from the right"). On this phrase there are three opinions.

The first: you used to overpower us by your power over us, because you were mightier than us. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: from the direction of religion, so that you misguide us away from it. This was said by al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) said: you come to us from the direction of religion, so you deceive us with the strongest of means.

The third: you used to confirm what you were saying with your oaths, so you came to us from the direction of the oaths you swore. This was related by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi. Then those who were followed say to them: ﴿بَلْ لَمْ تَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Rather, you were not believers"), meaning: you were not upon the truth, so that we could mislead you away from it. Rather, disbelief came from you.

﴿وَما كانَ لَنا عَلَيْكم مِن سُلْطانٍ﴾ ("We had no authority over you"). On this there are two opinions. The first: it means compulsion. The second: it means proof. According to the first, the meaning is: we had no power over you by which we could compel you, and force you to follow us.

(p-٥٥) According to the second, the meaning is: we did not bring you any proof for what we called you to, as the Messengers brought.

His words: ﴿فَحَقَّ عَلَيْنا قَوْلُ رَبِّنا﴾ ("So the word of our Lord has come due against us"), meaning: the word of punishment became binding upon us, which is His saying: ﴿لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("I will surely fill Hell") [al-A'raf: 18]. ﴿إنّا لَذائِقُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, we will taste the punishment"), all of us, you and we. ﴿فَأغْوَيْناكُمْ﴾ ("So we misled you"), meaning: we led you astray from guidance by calling you to what we were upon. This is His saying: ﴿إنّا كُنّا غاوِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, we were ourselves astray").

Then He informs about the followers and the followed with His saying: ﴿فَإنَّهم يَوْمَئِذٍ في العَذابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾ ("So indeed, that Day they will be sharers in the punishment"). Here, the criminals (al-mujrimun) are the polytheists. ﴿إنَّهم كانُوا﴾ ("Indeed, they used to be") in the world ﴿إذا قِيلَ لَهم لا إلَهَ إلا اللَّهُ﴾ ("when it was said to them: There is no god but Allah"), meaning: say this statement, ﴿يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ﴾ ("they were arrogant"), meaning: they magnified themselves against saying it. ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ أإنّا لَتارِكُو آلِهَتِنا﴾ ("And they said: Shall we really abandon our gods"), meaning: shall we abandon the worship of our gods ﴿لِشاعِرٍ﴾ ("for a poet")? That is, for following a poet?! They meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Allah answered them, saying: ﴿بَلْ﴾ ("Rather"), meaning: the matter is not as they said. Rather, ﴿جاءَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ ("he brought the truth"), which is the Tawhid and the Qur'an, ﴿وَصَدَّقَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ ("and confirmed the Messengers") who were before him. The meaning is that he came with what they came with. Then He addressed the polytheists with what promises this, up to His saying: ﴿إلا عِبادَ اللَّهِ المُخْلَصِينَ﴾ ("except the sincere servants of Allah"), meaning the monotheists. Abu Ubayda said: the Arabs say: "Indeed you are going, except Zayd." Regarding what is excepted from it, there are two opinions.

The first: it is excepted from the requital for deeds. The meaning is: we do not hold them accountable for their evil deeds; rather, we forgive them. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is excepted from the punishment. The meaning is: they will not taste the punishment. This was said by Muqatil.

His words: ﴿أُولَئِكَ لَهم رِزْقٌ مَعْلُومٌ﴾ ("For those there is a known provision"). On this there are two opinions. The first: it is Paradise, said by Qatada. The second: it is the provision in Paradise, said by al-Suddi.

(p-٥٦) According to this, regarding the meaning of "known" (ma'lum) there are two opinions. The first: it is according to the measure of morning and evening, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: when they desire it, it is brought to them, said by Muqatil.

Then He explained the provision, saying: ﴿فَواكِهُ﴾ ("fruits") [which is the plural of fakihah], and these are all fruits, fresh and dried. ﴿وَهم مُكْرَمُونَ﴾ ("and they will be honored") by what Allah has given them. What follows this has already been explained [al-Hijr: 47], up to His saying: ﴿يُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ ("A cup from a flowing spring will be passed around to them"). Al-Dahhak said: every cup mentioned in the Qur'an, by it is meant wine. [Abu Ubayda said: the kas (cup) is the vessel with what is in it, and al-mu'ayyan is clean running water. Al-Zajjaj said: the kas is the vessel in which there is wine.] The word kas applies to any vessel together with its drink; if it is empty, it is not a kas. Al-Mu'ayyan is wine that flows as water flows over the surface of the earth from springs.

His words: ﴿بَيْضاءَ﴾ ("white"). Al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: what indicates that by the cup He meant the wine is that He said "bayda'" (feminine), and if He had meant the vessel alone, or the vessel and the wine, He would have said "abyad" (masculine). Ibn Jarir said: by His words "bayda'" He meant the cup, and because the cup is feminine, "bayda'" was made feminine.

His words: ﴿لَذَّةٍ﴾ ("delicious"). Ibn Qutayba said: meaning delicious; it is said: "a drink of ladhadh" when it is pleasant. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning possessing delight.

﴿لا فِيها غَوْلٌ﴾ ("in which is no harm") has seven opinions.

The first: there is no headache in it, narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

The second: there is no stomach ache in it [narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said likewise].

(p-٥٧) The third: there is no headache in it, said by Qatada.

The fourth: there is nothing in it that is harmful or disliked, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: it does not seize their intellects, said by al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: it does not seize their minds so as to take them away, and no pain afflicts them from it.

The sixth: there is no sin in it, related by Ibn Jarir.

The seventh: there is none of these afflictions in it, because whoever is affected by any of these afflictions is said: "a ghawl has seized him." So the correct view is that the negation of ghawl from it encompasses all of these things. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

His words: ﴿وَلا هم عَنْها يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ ("nor will they be made drunk by it"). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the zay here and in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. 'Asim read it with a fatha on the zay here, and with a kasra in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the zay in both surahs. Al-Farra' said: whoever reads with a fatha, the meaning is: their intellects will not be taken away by drinking it. It is said of the drunk: "nazif" and "manzuf". Whoever reads with a kasra, there are two meanings: the first: they will not exhaust their drink, meaning it is perpetual forever. The second: they will not become drunk. The poet said:

"By my life, if you have been drained or have become sober,
you were the worst companions, the family of Ab-jar."

His words: ﴿وَعِنْدَهم قاصِراتُ الطَّرْفِ﴾ ("And with them will be women restraining their glances"). On this there are two opinions.

The first: they are women who have restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not look at anyone else. The root of qasr is confinement. Ibn Zayd said: a woman among them would say to her husband: "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you. Praise be to Allah who made me your wife and made you my husband."

The second: they have restricted the gaze of the husbands away from others, because of their perfect beauty. I heard this from our shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn al-Khashshab, the grammarian.

Regarding the word "eye" (ayn) there are three opinions. The first: they have beautiful eyes, said by Mujahid. The second: they have large eyes, said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. The third: they have large and beautiful eyes, and their singular is ʿaynaʾ, said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: there is no stomach ache in it [narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said likewise].

(p-٥٧) The third: there is no headache in it, said by Qatada.

The fourth: there is nothing in it that is harmful or disliked, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: it does not seize their intellects, said by al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: it does not seize their minds so as to take them away, and no pain afflicts them from it.

The sixth: there is no sin in it, related by Ibn Jarir.

The seventh: there is none of these afflictions in it, because whoever is affected by any of these afflictions is said: "a ghawl has seized him." So the correct view is that the negation of ghawl from it encompasses all of these things. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

His words: ﴿وَلا هم عَنْها يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ ("nor will they be made drunk by it"). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the zay here and in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. 'Asim read it with a fatha on the zay here, and with a kasra in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the zay in both surahs. Al-Farra' said: whoever reads with a fatha, the meaning is: their intellects will not be taken away by drinking it. It is said of the drunk: "nazif" and "manzuf". Whoever reads with a kasra, there are two meanings: the first: they will not exhaust their drink, meaning it is perpetual forever. The second: they will not become drunk. The poet said:

"By my life, if you have been drained or have become sober,
you were the worst companions, the family of Ab-jar."

His words: ﴿وَعِنْدَهم قاصِراتُ الطَّرْفِ﴾ ("And with them will be women restraining their glances"). On this there are two opinions.

The first: they are women who have restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not look at anyone else. The root of qasr is confinement. Ibn Zayd said: a woman among them would say to her husband: "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you. Praise be to Allah who made me your wife and made you my husband."

The second: they have restricted the gaze of the husbands away from others, because of their perfect beauty. I heard this from our shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn al-Khashshab, the grammarian.

Regarding the word "eye" (ayn) there are three opinions. The first: they have beautiful eyes, said by Mujahid. The second: they have large eyes, said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. The third: they have large and beautiful eyes, and their singular is ʿaynaʾ, said by al-Zajjaj.

His words: ﴿كَأنَّهُنَّ بَيْضٌ مَكْنُونٌ﴾ ("as if they were protected eggs"). Regarding what is meant by "eggs" here, there are three opinions. The first: it is pearls, related by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, and Abu Ubayda said likewise.

The second: the eggs of the ostrich, said by al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj. A group of the people of language said: the Arabs liken a beautiful woman, in her whiteness and the goodness of her complexion, to the ostrich egg, and this is the most beautiful of women's complexions: that a woman be white with a tinge of yellow.

The third: it is the egg when it is peeled before hands touch it, said by al-Suddi. To this meaning went Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and Ibn Jarir.

As for "maknun" (protected), it means "preserved". According to the first opinion, it is protected within its shell. According to the second, it is protected by ostrich feathers. According to the third, it is protected by its shell.

And some of them turn to others, questioning one another (﴿وَأقْبَلَ بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾). There are two opinions about who this refers to. The first: the humans turn to the devils. The second: the followers turn to their leaders. ﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ means they question one another in rebuke, reproach and blame. The followers say to the leaders: "Why did you deceive us?" And the leaders say: "Why did you accept from us?" This is the meaning of His words: ﴿قالُوا﴾, meaning the followers say to those who were followed: ﴿إنَّكم كُنْتُمْ تَأْتُونَنا عَنِ اليَمِينِ﴾ ("You used to come to us from the right"). On this phrase there are three opinions.

The first: you used to overpower us by your power over us, because you were mightier than us. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: from the direction of religion, so that you misguide us away from it. This was said by al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) said: you come to us from the direction of religion, so you deceive us with the strongest of means.

The third: you used to confirm what you were saying with your oaths, so you came to us from the direction of the oaths you swore. This was related by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi. Then those who were followed say to them: ﴿بَلْ لَمْ تَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Rather, you were not believers"), meaning: you were not upon the truth, so that we could mislead you away from it. Rather, disbelief came from you.

﴿وَما كانَ لَنا عَلَيْكم مِن سُلْطانٍ﴾ ("We had no authority over you"). On this there are two opinions. The first: it means compulsion. The second: it means proof. According to the first, the meaning is: we had no power over you by which we could compel you, and force you to follow us.

(p-٥٥) According to the second, the meaning is: we did not bring you any proof for what we called you to, as the Messengers brought.

His words: ﴿فَحَقَّ عَلَيْنا قَوْلُ رَبِّنا﴾ ("So the word of our Lord has come due against us"), meaning: the word of punishment became binding upon us, which is His saying: ﴿لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("I will surely fill Hell") [al-A'raf: 18]. ﴿إنّا لَذائِقُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, we will taste the punishment"), all of us, you and we. ﴿فَأغْوَيْناكُمْ﴾ ("So we misled you"), meaning: we led you astray from guidance by calling you to what we were upon. This is His saying: ﴿إنّا كُنّا غاوِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, we were ourselves astray").

Then He informs about the followers and the followed with His saying: ﴿فَإنَّهم يَوْمَئِذٍ في العَذابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾ ("So indeed, that Day they will be sharers in the punishment"). The second: it is excepted from the punishment. The meaning is: they will not taste the punishment. This was said by Muqatil.

Then He explained the provision, saying: ﴿فَواكِهُ﴾ ("fruits") [which is the plural of fakihah], and these are all fruits, fresh and dried. ﴿وَهم مُكْرَمُونَ﴾ ("and they will be honored") by what Allah has given them. What follows this has already been explained [al-Hijr: 47], up to His saying: ﴿يُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ ("A cup from a flowing spring will be passed around to them"). Al-Mu'ayyan is wine that flows as water flows over the surface of the earth from springs.

The second: there is no stomach ache in it [narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said likewise].

(p-٥٧) The third: there is no headache in it, said by Qatada.

The fourth: there is nothing in it that is harmful or disliked, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: it does not seize their intellects, said by al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: it does not seize their minds so as to take them away, and no pain afflicts them from it.

The sixth: there is no sin in it, related by Ibn Jarir.

The seventh: there is none of these afflictions in it, because whoever is affected by any of these afflictions is said: "a ghawl has seized him." So the correct view is that the negation of ghawl from it encompasses all of these things. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

His words: ﴿وَلا هم عَنْها يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ ("nor will they be made drunk by it"). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the zay here and in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. 'Asim read it with a fatha on the zay here, and with a kasra in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the zay in both surahs. Al-Farra' said: whoever reads with a fatha, the meaning is: their intellects will not be taken away by drinking it. It is said of the drunk: "nazif" and "manzuf". Whoever reads with a kasra, there are two meanings: the first: they will not exhaust their drink, meaning it is perpetual forever. The second: they will not become drunk. The poet said:

"By my life, if you have been drained or have become sober,
you were the worst companions, the family of Ab-jar."

His words: ﴿وَعِنْدَهم قاصِراتُ الطَّرْفِ﴾ ("And with them will be women restraining their glances"). On this there are two opinions.

The first: they are women who have restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not look at anyone else. The root of qasr is confinement. Ibn Zayd said: a woman among them would say to her husband: "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you. Praise be to Allah who made me your wife and made you my husband."

The second: they have restricted the gaze of the husbands away from others, because of their perfect beauty. I heard this from our shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn al-Khashshab, the grammarian.

Regarding the word "eye" (ayn) there are three opinions. The first: they have beautiful eyes, said by Mujahid. The second: they have large eyes, said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. The third: they have large and beautiful eyes, and their singular is ʿaynaʾ, said by al-Zajjaj.

His words: ﴿كَأنَّهُنَّ بَيْضٌ مَكْنُونٌ﴾ ("as if they were protected eggs"). Regarding what is meant by "eggs" here, there are three opinions. The first: it is pearls, related by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, and Abu Ubayda said likewise.

The second: the eggs of the ostrich, said by al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj. A group of the people of language said: the Arabs liken a beautiful woman, in her whiteness and the goodness of her complexion, to the ostrich egg, and this is the most beautiful of women's complexions: that a woman be white with a tinge of yellow.

The third: it is the egg when it is peeled before hands touch it, said by al-Suddi. To this meaning went Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and Ibn Jarir.

As for "maknun" (protected), it means "preserved". According to the first opinion, it is protected within its shell. According to the second, it is protected by ostrich feathers. According to the third, it is protected by its shell.

And some of them turn to others, questioning one another (﴿وَأقْبَلَ بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾). There are two opinions about who this refers to. The first: the humans turn to the devils. The second: the followers turn to their leaders. ﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ means they question one another in rebuke, reproach and blame. The followers say to the leaders: "Why did you deceive us?" And the leaders say: "Why did you accept from us?" This is the meaning of His words: ﴿قالُوا﴾, meaning the followers say to those who were followed: ﴿إنَّكم كُنْتُمْ تَأْتُونَنا عَنِ اليَمِينِ﴾ ("You used to come to us from the right"). On this phrase there are three opinions.

The first: you used to overpower us by your power over us, because you were mightier than us. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: from the direction of religion, so that you misguide us away from it. This was said by al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) said: you come to us from the direction of religion, so you deceive us with the strongest of means.

The third: you used to confirm what you were saying with your oaths, so you came to us from the direction of the oaths you swore. This was related by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi. Then those who were followed say to them: ﴿بَلْ لَمْ تَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Rather, you were not believers"), meaning: you were not upon the truth, so that we could mislead you away from it. Rather, disbelief came from you.

﴿وَما كانَ لَنا عَلَيْكم مِن سُلْطانٍ﴾ ("We had no authority over you"). On this there are two opinions. The first: it means compulsion. The second: it means proof. According to the first, the meaning is: we had no power over you by which we could compel you, and force you to follow us.

(p-٥٥) According to the second, the meaning is: we did not bring you any proof for what we called you to, as the Messengers brought.

His words: ﴿فَحَقَّ عَلَيْنا قَوْلُ رَبِّنا﴾ ("So the word of our Lord has come due against us"), meaning: the word of punishment became binding upon us, which is His saying: ﴿لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("I will surely fill Hell") [al-A'raf: 18]. ﴿إنّا لَذائِقُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, we will taste the punishment"), all of us, you and we. ﴿فَأغْوَيْناكُمْ﴾ ("So we misled you"), meaning: we led you astray from guidance by calling you to what we were upon. This is His saying: ﴿إنّا كُنّا غاوِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, we were ourselves astray").

Then He informs about the followers and the followed with His saying: ﴿فَإنَّهم يَوْمَئِذٍ في العَذابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾ ("So indeed, that Day they will be sharers in the punishment"). The second: it is excepted from the punishment. The meaning is: they will not taste the punishment. This was said by Muqatil.

Then He explained the provision, saying: ﴿فَواكِهُ﴾ ("fruits") [which is the plural of fakihah], and these are all fruits, fresh and dried. ﴿وَهم مُكْرَمُونَ﴾ ("and they will be honored") by what Allah has given them. What follows this has already been explained [al-Hijr: 47], up to His saying: ﴿يُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ ("A cup from a flowing spring will be passed around to them"). Al-Mu'ayyan is wine that flows as water flows over the surface of the earth from springs.

(p-٥٦) According to this, regarding the meaning of "known" (ma'lum) there are two opinions. The first: it is according to the measure of morning and evening, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: when they desire it, it is brought to them, said by Muqatil.

Then He explained the provision, saying: ﴿فَواكِهُ﴾ ("fruits") [which is the plural of fakihah], and these are all fruits, fresh and dried. ﴿وَهم مُكْرَمُونَ﴾ ("and they will be honored") by what Allah has given them. What follows this has already been explained [al-Hijr: 47], up to His saying: ﴿يُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ ("A cup from a flowing spring will be passed around to them"). Al-Dahhak said: every cup mentioned in the Qur'an, by it is meant wine. [Abu Ubayda said: the kas (cup) is the vessel with what is in it, and al-mu'ayyan is clean running water. Al-Zajjaj said: the kas is the vessel in which there is wine.] The word kas applies to any vessel together with its drink; if it is empty, it is not a kas. Al-Mu'ayyan is wine that flows as water flows over the surface of the earth from springs.

His words: ﴿بَيْضاءَ﴾ ("white"). Al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: what indicates that by the cup He meant the wine is that He said "bayda'" (feminine), and if He had meant the vessel alone, or the vessel and the wine, He would have said "abyad" (masculine). Ibn Jarir said: by His words "bayda'" He meant the cup, and because the cup is feminine, "bayda'" was made feminine.

His words: ﴿لَذَّةٍ﴾ ("delicious"). Ibn Qutayba said: meaning delicious; it is said: "a drink of ladhadh" when it is pleasant. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning possessing delight.

﴿لا فِيها غَوْلٌ﴾ ("in which is no harm") has seven opinions.

The first: there is no headache in it, narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

The second: there is no stomach ache in it [narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said likewise].

(p-٥٧) The third: there is no headache in it, said by Qatada.

The fourth: there is nothing in it that is harmful or disliked, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: it does not seize their intellects, said by al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: it does not seize their minds so as to take them away, and no pain afflicts them from it.

The sixth: there is no sin in it, related by Ibn Jarir.

The seventh: there is none of these afflictions in it, because whoever is affected by any of these afflictions is said: "a ghawl has seized him." So the correct view is that the negation of ghawl from it encompasses all of these things. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

His words: ﴿وَلا هم عَنْها يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ ("nor will they be made drunk by it"). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the zay here and in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. 'Asim read it with a fatha on the zay here, and with a kasra in [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the zay in both surahs. Al-Farra' said: whoever reads with a fatha, the meaning is: their intellects will not be taken away by drinking it. It is said of the drunk: "nazif" and "manzuf". Whoever reads with a kasra, there are two meanings: the first: they will not exhaust their drink, meaning it is perpetual forever. The second: they will not become drunk. The poet said:

"By my life, if you have been drained or have become sober,
you were the worst companions, the family of Ab-jar."

His words: ﴿وَعِنْدَهم قاصِراتُ الطَّرْفِ﴾ ("And with them will be women restraining their glances"). On this there are two opinions.

The first: they are women who have restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not look at anyone else. The root of qasr is confinement. Ibn Zayd said: a woman among them would say to her husband: "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you. Praise be to Allah who made me your wife and made you my husband."

The second: they have restricted the gaze of the husbands away from others, because of their perfect beauty. I heard this from our shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn al-Khashshab, the grammarian.

Regarding the word "eye" (ayn) there are three opinions. The first: they have beautiful eyes, said by Mujahid. The second: they have large eyes, said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. The third: they have large and beautiful eyes, and their singular is ʿaynaʾ, said by al-Zajjaj.

His words: ﴿كَأنَّهُنَّ بَيْضٌ مَكْنُونٌ﴾ ("as if they were protected eggs"). Regarding what is meant by "eggs" here, there are three opinions. The first: it is pearls, related by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, and Abu Ubayda said likewise.

The second: the eggs of the ostrich, said by al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj. A group of the people of language said: the Arabs liken a beautiful woman, in her whiteness and the goodness of her complexion, to the ostrich egg, and this is the most beautiful of women's complexions: that a woman be white with a tinge of yellow.

The third: it is the egg when it is peeled before hands touch it, said by al-Suddi. To this meaning went Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and Ibn Jarir.

As for "maknun" (protected), it means "preserved". According to the first opinion, it is protected within its shell. According to the second, it is protected by ostrich feathers. According to the third, it is protected by its shell.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 37, verse 50–61:

(p-59) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they will turn to one another, questioning﴾ — meaning the people of Paradise — ﴿questioning one another﴾ about conditions they had in the world.

﴿A speaker among them will say: Indeed, I had a companion﴾. Concerning this (qarin, "companion") there are four opinions. The first: that he was a companion in the world. The second: that he was a partner (sharik), related from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: that he was Satan, said by Mujahid. The fourth: that he was a brother; Muqatil said: "They are the two brothers mentioned in Surat al-Kahf [18:32] in His saying: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men﴾." The meaning is: I had a companion or brother who denies the Resurrection, ﴿who says: Are you indeed among those who affirm?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: it is with a light (mukhaffafa) sad, from sidq, yusaddiqu, so he is musaddiq, and it is not permissible here to double the sad. The commentators said: the meaning is: "Are you indeed among those who affirm the Resurrection?" Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Qadi related from Hamzah reading "al-musaddiqin" with a doubled sad.

(p-60) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Are we indeed to be held accountable?﴾ That is: we will be recompensed for our deeds; it is said: "dintuhu bima sana'a," meaning: I repaid him for what he did. So the believer wished to see the companion of the disbeliever, and said to the people of Paradise: ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ That is: would you like to look down into the Fire, so that you may know where your station is relative to the station of its people? Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu 'Imran, and Ibn Ya'mur read "hal antum muttali'un" with a sukun on the ta' and lightened. ﴿So he looked down﴾ with a raised hamza and a sukun on the ta'. Abu Razin and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "mutti'un" with a kasra on the nun. Ibn Mas'ud said: "He looked down, then turned to his companions and said: 'I have seen the skulls of the people boiling.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: that is because in Paradise there are openings through which its people look at the Fire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he saw him﴾ — meaning the companion of the disbeliever — ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, in its middle. It was said: the middle was called sawa' only because the distance from it to the sides is equal. Khulayd al-'Asri said: "By God, were it not that God had made him know it, he would not have recognized him; his features had changed and his form." Then ﴿He said: By God, you nearly brought me to ruin﴾. The commentators said: its meaning: "By God, I was only about to be destroyed by you"; it is said "ardaytu fulanan," meaning: I destroyed him. ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord﴾ — that is, His bestowal upon me of Islam — ﴿I would have been among those brought forth﴾ with you into the Fire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then are we not to die﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: that when death is slaughtered, the people of Paradise will say: "Then are we not to die, (p-61) except our first death" which was in the world? ﴿And we will not be punished?﴾ It will be said to them: No. Then they will say: ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾, and God the Exalted will say: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It was also said: He says that to the angels.

The second: that it is the believer's saying to his companions, and they said to him: "You will not die," and he said: "Indeed, this is the great triumph." This was said by Muqatil. Abu Sufyan al-Dimashqi said: the believer addressed the people of Paradise with this out of joy at the enduring of bliss, not as a question, since he knew they would not die; rather he repeated the words so that their repetition would increase his joy upon hearing them.

The third: that it is the believer's saying to his disbelieving companion, by way of rebuke for what he used to deny; mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the like of this﴾ — meaning the bliss He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those will have a known provision﴾ [37:41] — ﴿let the workers work﴾. This is an encouragement to seek God's reward, the Mighty and Majestic, through obedience to Him.

The second: that he was a partner (sharik), related from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: that he was Satan, said by Mujahid. The fourth: that he was a brother; Muqatil said: "They are the two brothers mentioned in Surat al-Kahf [18:32] in His saying: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men﴾." The meaning is: I had a companion or brother who denies the Resurrection, ﴿who says: Are you indeed among those who affirm?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: it is with a light (mukhaffafa) sad, from sidq, yusaddiqu, so he is musaddiq, and it is not permissible here to double the sad. The commentators said: the meaning is: "Are you indeed among those who affirm the Resurrection?" Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Qadi related from Hamzah reading "al-musaddiqin" with a doubled sad.

(p-60) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Are we indeed to be held accountable?﴾ That is: we will be recompensed for our deeds; it is said: "dintuhu bima sana'a," meaning: I repaid him for what he did. So the believer wished to see the companion of the disbeliever, and said to the people of Paradise: ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ That is: would you like to look down into the Fire, so that you may know where your station is relative to the station of its people? Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu 'Imran, and Ibn Ya'mur read "hal antum muttali'un" with a sukun on the ta' and lightened. ﴿So he looked down﴾ with a raised hamza and a sukun on the ta'. Abu Razin and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "mutti'un" with a kasra on the nun. Ibn Mas'ud said: "He looked down, then turned to his companions and said: 'I have seen the skulls of the people boiling.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: that is because in Paradise there are openings through which its people look at the Fire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he saw him﴾ — meaning the companion of the disbeliever — ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, in its middle. It was said: the middle was called sawa' only because the distance from it to the sides is equal. Khulayd al-'Asri said: "By God, were it not that God had made him know it, he would not have recognized him; his features had changed and his form." Then ﴿He said: By God, you nearly brought me to ruin﴾. The commentators said: its meaning: "By God, I was only about to be destroyed by you"; it is said "ardaytu fulanan," meaning: I destroyed him. ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord﴾ — that is, His bestowal upon me of Islam — ﴿I would have been among those brought forth﴾ with you into the Fire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then are we not to die﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: that when death is slaughtered, the people of Paradise will say: "Then are we not to die, (p-61) except our first death" which was in the world? ﴿And we will not be punished?﴾ It will be said to them: No. Then they will say: ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾, and God the Exalted will say: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It was also said: He says that to the angels.

The second: that it is the believer's saying to his companions, and they said to him: "You will not die," and he said: "Indeed, this is the great triumph." This was said by Muqatil. Abu Sufyan al-Dimashqi said: the believer addressed the people of Paradise with this out of joy at the enduring of bliss, not as a question, since he knew they would not die; rather he repeated the words so that their repetition would increase his joy upon hearing them.

The third: that it is the believer's saying to his disbelieving companion, by way of rebuke for what he used to deny; mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the like of this﴾ — meaning the bliss He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those will have a known provision﴾ [37:41] — ﴿let the workers work﴾. This is an encouragement to seek God's reward, the Mighty and Majestic, through obedience to Him.

(p-63) Is that better as a hospitable provision (nuzul), or the tree of zaqqum? Ibn Qutaybah said: "Nuzul means provision (rizq). This is what is meant by ﴿or the tree of zaqqum?﴾

Others said: "The zaqqum is the fruit of a tree whose taste is disgusting." The third: the trial means testing. They were tested by it and so they denied, as said by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Hasan said: "Its root is at the bottom of the Fire, and its branches rise up to its levels." ﴿Its spathes﴾, that is, its fruit, and it is called ṭal‘ (spathe) because it emerges (ṭuluʿ). ﴿It is as if its spathes were the heads of devils.﴾

If it is asked: how did He liken it to something that has not been seen? There are three answers to this.

The first: the ugliness of devils is firmly established in souls, even though they are not seen, so it is permissible to liken it to something whose ugliness is known. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Will he kill me while the sharp sword is my bedfellow,
and the sharpened blue blades are like the fangs of ghouls?"

Abu Ubaydah said: "The Arabs say: everything you mix with something else is mashub (mixed)." The commentators said: when they eat the zaqqum and then drink the boiling water on top of it, the boiling water mixes with the zaqqum in their bellies, becoming a mixture for it.

If it is asked: how did He liken it to something that has not been seen? There are three answers to this.

The first: the ugliness of devils is firmly established in souls, even though they are not seen, so it is permissible to liken it to something whose ugliness is known. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Will he kill me while the sharp sword is my bedfellow,
and the sharpened blue blades are like the fangs of ghouls?"

Al-Zajjaj said: "He had not seen the ghoul or its fangs. But comparing with what is considered repulsive is more eloquent. For the masculine it is compared to devils, and for the feminine it is compared to the ghoul."

The second: between Makkah and Yemen there is a tree called "the heads of devils," and He likened it to that. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

(p-64) The third: He meant by "devils" snakes that have heads and crests. He likened its spathe to the heads of snakes. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: "The Arabs call some snakes a shaytan, and it is a snake with a crest and an ugly face."

God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed they will eat from it﴾, that is, from its fruit, ﴿and fill their bellies with it﴾. This is because they will be compelled to eat it until their bellies are filled.

﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water.﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: "That is, a blend of hot water which they drink upon it." Abu Ubaydah said: "The Arabs say: everything you mix with something else is mashub (mixed)." The commentators said: when they eat the zaqqum and then drink the boiling water on top of it, the boiling water mixes with the zaqqum in their bellies, becoming a mixture for it.

﴿Then indeed their return﴾, that is, after eating the zaqqum and drinking the boiling water, ﴿is surely to the Hellfire.﴾ That is because the boiling water is outside the Hellfire, so they are driven to it as camels are driven to water, and then they are returned to the Hellfire. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿going around between it and scalding water﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 44]. ﴿Found﴾ means "found." ﴿Rushing﴾ is explained at [Hud: 78], and the meaning is that they follow their fathers in haste. ﴿And certainly most of the earlier people had gone astray before them﴾, that is, before these polytheists, from the past nations.

(p-65) God the Exalted says: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾, meaning the monotheists, for they were saved from the punishment. Ibn Jarir said: "The exception is good because the meaning is: look how We destroyed the warners, except the servants of Allah."

(p-63) Is that better as a hospitable provision (nuzul), or the tree of zaqqum? Ibn Qutaybah said: "Nuzul means provision (rizq). From it comes the phrase iqamat al-inzal, and inzal al-junud means their provisions." Al-Zajjaj said: "Nuzul here means abundance and surplus. It is said: 'This is food that has nuzl and nuzul,' with the z pronounced both with sukun and with damma. The meaning of ﴿Is that better?﴾ is: is that better as a kind of hospitality by which one is sustained and can remain, or the hospitality of the people of the Fire?" This is what is meant by ﴿or the tree of zaqqum?﴾

The scholars differed over whether this tree exists in this world or not. Qutrub said: "It is a bitter tree found in the land of Tihamah, one of the most foul of trees." Others said: "The zaqqum is the fruit of a tree whose taste is disgusting." It was also said: "It is not known among the trees of this world; it is in the Fire, and the people of the Fire are forced to eat from it."

God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the disbelievers. There are three opinions regarding what is meant by the trial.

The first: when Allah mentioned that it is in the Fire, they were tested and denied, saying: "How can there be a tree in the Fire, when the Fire consumes trees?" So this verse was revealed. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Suddi said: it was a trial for Abu Jahl and his companions.

The second: the trial means punishment. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: the trial means testing. They were tested by it and so they denied, as said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿And Noah certainly called out to Us﴾, that is, he called upon Us. There are two views about the content of his supplication. The first is that he called for help against his people. The second is that he asked Us to save him from drowning. ﴿And excellent are the Responders﴾, Us; the meaning is: We saved him and destroyed his people.

Regarding ﴿the great distress﴾, there are two views. The first is that it refers to drowning. The second is the harm inflicted on him by his people.

﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾. [That is] because the offspring of the people of the Ark perished, except the offspring of his sons, so all people are descended from Noah. ﴿And We left for him﴾, that is, We left for him a good remembrance ﴿among later generations﴾, who are those who came after him until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: That good remembrance is His saying: ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾, and those who came after him (p-66). Muqatil said: God rewarded him for his goodness with a fine praise among the worlds.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham﴾, meaning: among the people of his religion and creed. The pronoun in "his followers" refers to Noah according to most scholars. Ibn al-Sa'ib said it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), and al-Farra' chose this view.

(p-٦٧) If it is asked: how can he be among his followers when he came before him?

The answer: it is like His saying: ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41], where He called them their offspring although they came before them. We have explained this earlier [Ya-Sin: 41].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When he came to his Lord﴾, meaning: he affirmed Allah and believed in Him, ﴿with a sound heart﴾, free from polytheism and every impurity. There are sayings about this which we mentioned under [ash-Shu'ara': 89].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿What do you worship?﴾ This is a question of rebuke, as if he were reproaching them for worshipping other than Allah. ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah?﴾ meaning: do you invent a lie and worship gods besides Allah? ﴿So what is your assumption about the Lord of the worlds?﴾ — when you meet Him after having worshipped others? As if he said: what do you assume He will do to you?

﴿Then he glanced at the stars﴾. There are two views on this.

One of them: he looked into the science of the stars (ʿilm al-nujum, astrology). These people practised the science of the stars, so he dealt with them on their own terms and showed them that he knew of that what they knew, so that they would not object to him. Ibn al-Musayyab said: he saw a rising star and said: "I am ill tomorrow."

The second: he looked at the stars, not into their science.

If it is asked: what was his purpose?

The answer: they had a festival, and he wanted to stay behind from them in order to plot against their idols, so he gave this saying as an excuse.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿I am sick﴾. This is one of the indirect expressions (ma'arid al-kalam). There are then three views.

One of them: its meaning is "I will become sick." This was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn al-Anbari said: Allah the Exalted informed him that He would test him with sickness when a star rose that he knew; when he saw the star, he knew that he would become sick.

(p-٦٨) The second: "I am sick at heart over you, since you seek prognostication from stars that neither harm nor benefit." Mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: he was sick from an ailment that befell him. Related by al-Mawardi. al-Suddi mentioned that he went out with them to their festival day, and when he was on part of the road, he threw himself down and said: "I am sick, my leg hurts." ﴿So they turned their backs and went away﴾. ﴿Then he turned secretly to their gods﴾, meaning: he inclined towards them — they had placed food before them so that it would be blessed, according to their claim — ﴿and said﴾ Abraham, mocking them: ﴿Will you not eat?﴾

As for His saying: ﴿striking them with the right hand﴾, there are three views regarding "the right hand."

One: it is the right hand; this was said by al-Dahhak.

(p-٦٩) The second: with power and might; said by al-Suddi and al-Farra'.

The third: with the oath that had preceded from him, namely his saying: "By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols" [al-Anbiya': 57]; related by al-Mawardi.

Al-Zajjaj said: "striking" (darban) is a verbal noun; the meaning is: he turned upon the idols, striking them with the right hand. He said "upon them" although they are idols, because they had made them equivalent to those who discern.

﴿Then they came hastening towards him﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read yazaffūna with a fatha on the ya', a kasra on the za', and a shadda on the fa'. Hamza and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read yuzaffūna with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the za', and a shadda on the fa'. Ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Mutawakkil and al-Dahhak read yazaffūna with a fatha on the ya', a kasra on the za', and a light fa' (no shadda). Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu Nuhayk read yazuffūna with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the za', and a light fa'. Al-Zajjaj said: the most correct reading is the fatha on the ya' with a shadda on the fa'; its origin is from the zafif of ostriches, which is the beginning of the running of ostriches; one says zaffa al-na'am yazuffu. As for the damma on the ya', its meaning is: they come to the state of zafif. They quoted:

"Husayn wished to be master over his people, but Husayn became humiliated and subdued."

That is, he came to subjugation. As for the kasra on the za' with a light fa', it comes from: wuzzifa yuzaffu, meaning "hastened, rushes," which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' did not know, while others did.

(p-٧٠) The exegetes said: word reached them of what Abraham had done, so they hastened; when they arrived to him, he said to them, reasoning against them: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ with your own hands ﴿while Allah created you and what you make?﴾ Ibn Jarir said: regarding "ma" there are two possibilities.

One: that it means the verbal noun, so the meaning is: Allah created you and your work.

The second: that it means "that which", so the meaning is: Allah created you and the creation of that which you make with your hands from idols. In this verse is evidence that the actions of servants are created [by Allah].

When the proof bound them, ﴿they said: build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire﴾. We have explained his story in [al-Anbiya': 52–74], and clarified the meaning of "al-Jahim" in [al-Baqarah: 119], and the plot they intended: burning him.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿So We made them the lowest﴾ is that Abraham overcame them with proof, since Allah protected him from their plot and destruction befell them.

﴿And he said﴾, meaning Abraham: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord﴾. There are two views regarding this going.

One: he is truly going, and at the time of his saying this there are two views. One: when he intended to emigrate from his people; so the meaning is: I am going to where my Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded me. ﴿He will guide me﴾ to where He commanded me, which is Syria; said by most. The second: when he was cast into the fire; said by Sulayman ibn Surad. In this case, regarding the meaning there are two views: one: he is going to Allah by death, (p-٧١) and He will guide me to Paradise; the second: [going] to what my Lord has decreed, He will guide me to escape from the fire.

The second saying: "I am going to my Lord" with my heart, my deed and my intention; said by Qatadah.

Al-Zajjaj said: this glad tidings indicates that he was given good news of a male son, and that he would remain until he reached maturity and was described as forbearing.
