The second: that it means walking, and the meaning is that he walked with his father. This was said by Qatadah. Ibn Qutaybah said: he reached the point of going about with him and assisting him. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he was thirteen years old.

The third: that by "al-sa'y" is meant worship ('ibadah). This was said by Ibn Zayd; according to this, [the phrase] means he had reached [maturity].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾ — most scholars hold that he did not see in the dream that he had actually slaughtered him; rather the meaning is that he was commanded in the dream to slaughter him. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Some have held that he saw himself treating (attempting) his slaughter, but did not see the shedding of blood. Qatadah said: The dreams of the prophets are true; when they see something, they do it. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs that when Jibril gave Sarah the good news of a child, Ibrahim said: "Then he is a sacrifice for Allah." When he finished building the House, he was visited in a dream and it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." They differed about who the one to be sacrificed was, on two views.

One of them: [that it was] Isaac. This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Wahb ibn Munabbih, [and Masruq], 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, and Muqatil ibn Sulayman, and Ibn Jarir chose it. These say: this story took place in the Levant (al-Sham). It is said: the earth was folded up for him until he carried him to the place of sacrifice at Mina in an hour.

The second: that it was Isma'il. This was said by Ibn 'Umar, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, al-Hasan al-Basri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Yusuf ibn Mihran, Abu Salih, (p-73) Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit. The reports from Ibn 'Abbas differ: 'Ikrimah related from him that it was Isaac, while 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Jawza', and Yusuf ibn Mihran related from him that it was Isma'il. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from him both views. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, and al-Suddi there are two reports. Likewise from Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, there are two reports. Each group has its proof, which is not the place for it, and our companions support the first view.

Reference to the story of the sacrifice

The people of learning in biography (siyar) and exegesis (tafsir) mention that when Ibrahim intended to slaughter his son, he said to him: "Set out, so that we may offer a sacrifice to Allah, Mighty and Majestic." He took a knife and a rope, then they set out, until when they went between the mountains, the boy said to him: "O father, where is your sacrifice?" He said: "O my son, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you." The boy said to him: "Tighten my bonds so that I do not thrash about, and keep your clothes away from me so that none of my blood splashes on you and your mother sees it and grieves, and hasten the passage of the knife over my throat so that death may be easier for me. When you come to my mother, convey my greetings to her." Ibrahim came to him, kissing him and weeping, and said: "What a good helper you are, O my son, in the matter of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." (p-74)(p-75) Then he drew the knife over his throat, but it did not cut anything. Mujahid said: When he drew it over his throat, it turned over, so he said: "What is wrong with you?" It had turned over. He said: "Stab with it, a stabbing blow." Al-Suddi said: Allah placed a sheet of copper over his throat; but this is not needed, since preventing it by power is more eloquent. They said: when he stabbed with it, it [the throat] grew back, and Allah knew from both of them the truthfulness in submission. So he was called: "O Ibrahim, you have indeed fulfilled the vision. This is the ransom for your son." Ibrahim looked, and behold, Jibril was with him with a white ram with black markings.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then consider what you think﴾ — he did not say that in the manner of consulting about the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but wanted to see what opinion he had. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "mādhā turī" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the ra'; and regarding it there are two views. One: "what do you show me of your patience or your anxiety," said al-Farra'. The second: "what has become clear," said al-Zajjaj. Others said: "what do you suggest."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: do what has been revealed to you concerning my slaughter. ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the patient﴾ — in the face of trial.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted﴾ — i.e., they surrendered to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, obeyed and were content. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "falammā sallamā" with the lam doubled and without a hamzah before the sin; the meaning: they both submitted to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Regarding the response to His saying "So when they both submitted," there are two views.

One: that its response is "and We called to him," and the waw is extra; said al-Farra'.

The second: that the response is omitted because the speech contains an indication of it; the meaning: when they did that, he was made prosperous and his reward was multiplied; said al-Zajjaj.

(p-76) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ — Ibn Qutaybah said: i.e., he laid him down on his brow, so that one of his two temples was on the ground. The two temples (jabinan) are on either side, and the forehead (jabhah) lies between them, which is what strikes the ground in prostration. People hardly distinguish between the jabin and the jabhah; the jabhah is the place of a man where the mark of prostration appears, and the two temples flank it, one on each side.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We called to him﴾ — the commentators said: he was called from the mountain: ﴿O Ibrahim﴾ ﴿you have indeed fulfilled the vision﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One: "you have indeed carried out what you were commanded," since he intended the slaughter to the extent he was able, and the son obeyed him by allowing himself to be slaughtered; but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, turned that away as He willed, so it became as though he had slaughtered, even though the slaughter was not actually completed.

The second: that he saw in the dream the process of slaughtering but did not see the shedding of blood; so when he did in wakefulness what he had seen in the dream, it was said to him: "you have indeed fulfilled the vision."

Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', Abu 'Imran, and al-Jahdari read "qad saddaqta al-ru'ya" with the dal lightened, and here the speech is complete. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, thus⟩ — i.e., as We have mentioned of pardoning him from slaughtering his son — ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾.

(p-77) ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest trial﴾ — regarding this there are two views. One: the manifest blessings, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The second: the great test, said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn Qutaybah. According to the first, his saying "this" refers to the pardon from slaughter; according to the second, it refers to his being tested by the sacrifice of his son.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We ransomed him﴾ — meaning: the one who was to be slaughtered ﴿with a great sacrifice﴾. "Dhibh" with a kasrah on the dhal is the name of what is slaughtered; with a fathah on the dhal it is the verbal noun of "dhabahtu," said Ibn Qutaybah. The meaning of the verse: We delivered him from slaughter by making the sacrifice a ransom for him. Regarding this sacrifice there are three views.

One: that it was a horned ram which had grazed in Paradise for forty years before that; said Ibn 'Abbas in the report of Mujahid, and in the report of Sa'id ibn Jubayr he said: it is the ram which Adam's son offered, which was accepted from him, and it was in Paradise until it was ransomed with it.

The second: that Ibrahim ransomed his son with two white, large-eyed, horned rams; narrated by Abu al-Tufayl from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: [that it was] ransomed only with a male mountain goat (tays min al-awra), sent down upon him from Thabir; said al-Hasan.

Regarding the meaning of "great" (·aẓīm) there are four views.

One: because it had grazed in Paradise; said Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

(p-78) The second: because it was slaughtered in accordance with the religion and sunnah of Ibrahim; said al-Hasan.

The third: because it was accepted; said Mujahid. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: when Adam's son offered it, it was lifted up alive, grazed in Paradise, and then it was made the ransom for the sacrifice, and so it was accepted twice.

The fourth: because of its great form and blessing; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We left upon him﴾ — we have explained it in this surah [al-Saffat: 78].

Reference to the story of the sacrifice

The reports from Ibn 'Abbas differ: 'Ikrimah related from him that it was Isaac, while 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Jawza', and Yusuf ibn Mihran related from him that it was Isma'il. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from him both views. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, and al-Suddi there are two reports. Likewise from Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, there are two reports. Each group has its proof, which is not the place for it, and our companions support the first view.

Reference to the story of the sacrifice

The people of learning in biography (siyar) and exegesis (tafsir) mention that when Ibrahim intended to slaughter his son, he said to him: "Set out, so that we may offer a sacrifice to Allah, Mighty and Majestic." He took a knife and a rope, then they set out, until when they went between the mountains, the boy said to him: "O father, where is your sacrifice?" He said: "O my son, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you." The boy said to him: "Tighten my bonds so that I do not thrash about, and keep your clothes away from me so that none of my blood splashes on you and your mother sees it and grieves, and hasten the passage of the knife over my throat so that death may be easier for me. When you come to my mother, convey my greetings to her." Ibrahim came to him, kissing him and weeping, and said: "What a good helper you are, O my son, in the matter of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." (p-74)(p-75) Then he drew the knife over his throat, but it did not cut anything. Mujahid said: When he drew it over his throat, it turned over, so he said: "What is wrong with you?" It had turned over. He said: "Stab with it, a stabbing blow." Al-Suddi said: Allah placed a sheet of copper over his throat; but this is not needed, since preventing it by power is more eloquent. They said: when he stabbed with it, it [the throat] grew back, and Allah knew from both of them the truthfulness in submission. So he was called: "O Ibrahim, you have indeed fulfilled the vision. This is the ransom for your son." Ibrahim looked, and behold, Jibril was with him with a white ram with black markings.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then consider what you think﴾ — he did not say that in the manner of consulting about the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but wanted to see what opinion he had. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "mādhā turī" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the ra'; and regarding it there are two views. One: "what do you show me of your patience or your anxiety," said al-Farra'. The second: "what has become clear," said al-Zajjaj. Others said: "what do you suggest."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: do what has been revealed to you concerning my slaughter. ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the patient﴾ — in the face of trial.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted﴾ — i.e., they surrendered to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, obeyed and were content. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "falammā sallamā" with the lam doubled and without a hamzah before the sin; the meaning: they both submitted to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Regarding the response to His saying "So when they both submitted," there are two views.

One: that its response is "and We called to him," and the waw is extra; said al-Farra'.

The second: that the response is omitted because the speech contains an indication of it; the meaning: when they did that, he was made prosperous and his reward was multiplied; said al-Zajjaj.

(p-76) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ — Ibn Qutaybah said: i.e., he laid him down on his brow, so that one of his two temples was on the ground. The two temples (jabinan) are on either side, and the forehead (jabhah) lies between them, which is what strikes the ground in prostration. People hardly distinguish between the jabin and the jabhah; the jabhah is the place of a man where the mark of prostration appears, and the two temples flank it, one on each side.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We called to him﴾ — the commentators said: he was called from the mountain: ﴿O Ibrahim﴾ ﴿you have indeed fulfilled the vision﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One: "you have indeed carried out what you were commanded," since he intended the slaughter to the extent he was able, and the son obeyed him by allowing himself to be slaughtered; but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, turned that away as He willed, so it became as though he had slaughtered, even though the slaughter was not actually completed.

The second: that he saw in the dream the process of slaughtering but did not see the shedding of blood; so when he did in wakefulness what he had seen in the dream, it was said to him: "you have indeed fulfilled the vision."

Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', Abu 'Imran, and al-Jahdari read "qad saddaqta al-ru'ya" with the dal lightened, and here the speech is complete. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, thus⟩ — i.e., as We have mentioned of pardoning him from slaughtering his son — ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾.

(p-77) ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest trial﴾ — regarding this there are two views. One: the manifest blessings, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The second: the great test, said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn Qutaybah. According to the first, his saying "this" refers to the pardon from slaughter; according to the second, it refers to his being tested by the sacrifice of his son.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We ransomed him﴾ — meaning: the one who was to be slaughtered ﴿with a great sacrifice﴾. "Dhibh" with a kasrah on the dhal is the name of what is slaughtered; with a fathah on the dhal it is the verbal noun of "dhabahtu," said Ibn Qutaybah. The meaning of the verse: We delivered him from slaughter by making the sacrifice a ransom for him. Regarding this sacrifice there are three views.

One: that it was a horned ram which had grazed in Paradise for forty years before that; said Ibn 'Abbas in the report of Mujahid, and in the report of Sa'id ibn Jubayr he said: it is the ram which Adam's son offered, which was accepted from him, and it was in Paradise until it was ransomed with it.

The second: that Ibrahim ransomed his son with two white, large-eyed, horned rams; narrated by Abu al-Tufayl from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: [that it was] ransomed only with a male mountain goat (tays min al-awra), sent down upon him from Thabir; said al-Hasan.

Regarding the meaning of "great" (·aẓīm) there are four views.

One: because it had grazed in Paradise; said Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

(p-78) The second: because it was slaughtered in accordance with the religion and sunnah of Ibrahim; said al-Hasan.

The third: because it was accepted; said Mujahid. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: when Adam's son offered it, it was lifted up alive, grazed in Paradise, and then it was made the ransom for the sacrifice, and so it was accepted twice.

The fourth: because of its great form and blessing; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We left upon him﴾ — we have explained it in this surah [al-Saffat: 78].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾ — whoever says that Isaac is the one who was to be sacrificed says: He gave Ibrahim the good news of the prophethood of Isaac, and Isaac was rewarded with prophethood for his patience. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas in the report of 'Ikrimah, and it was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Whoever says the one to be sacrificed was Isma'il says: Allah gave Ibrahim the good news of a son who would be a prophet after this story, as a reward for his obedience and patience. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾ — meaning by the multiplication of their offspring, and they are all the tribes (asbat); ﴿And of their offspring is one who does good﴾ — i.e., obedient to Allah; ﴿and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾ — and he is the one who disobeys Him. It was also said: the one who does good is the believer, and the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever.

(p-79) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon Moses and Aaron﴾ — that is, We bestowed upon them both prophethood.

Regarding ﴿the great distress﴾ there are two views. One is the enslavement of Pharaoh and his trials, which is the meaning of the statement of Qatada. The second is the drowning, as said by al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We helped them﴾ — there are two views concerning it. One is that it refers to Moses, Aaron and their people. The second is that it refers to the two of them alone, and it is put in the plural because the Arabs refer to a leader with the plural, to include his soldiers and followers; this was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. As for what follows, its explanation has already preceded [al-Anbiya: 48], up to His saying: ﴿And indeed Elias was among the messengers﴾ — concerning it there are two views.

One: he was a prophet from among the prophets of the Children of Israel, as said by the majority.

The second: he is Idris, as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada; and so Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Aliya and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi used to recite: "And indeed Idris" in place of "Ilyas".

(p-80) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he said to his people: Will you not fear Allah?﴾ — that is, will you not fear Allah so that you single Him out and worship Him?! ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l﴾ — concerning it there are three views.

One: it means "Lord", as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba. al-Dahhak said: Ibn 'Abbas had been perplexed by this word, and while he was sitting, a Bedouin passed by whose she-camel had strayed, and he was saying: "Who has found a she-camel of which I am the ba'l?" The boys followed him shouting at him: "O husband of the she-camel, O husband of the she-camel!" So Ibn 'Abbas called him and said: "Woe to you, what did you mean by its ba'l?" He said: "I am its lord." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah has spoken the truth: 'Do you call upon Ba'l' — a lord." Qatada said: this is a Yemeni dialect.

The second: it is the name of an idol they had, as said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jarir related that Ba'labakk was named after it.

The third: it is a woman whom they used to worship, related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah, your Lord﴾ — Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "Allahu Rabbukum" with the nominative. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, Khalaf and Ya'qub read "Allaha" with the accusative.

(p-81) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forward﴾ — to the Fire; ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ — those who did not deny him, for they will not be brought to the Fire.

Reference to the story

The people of knowledge in tafsir and the biographies have mentioned that when the events multiplied after the passing of the Prophet Ezekiel (peace be upon him), and idols were worshipped, Allah the Exalted sent Elias to them. Ibn Ishaq said: he was Elias son of Tishbi, son of Finhas, son of al-'Ayzar, son of Aaron son of 'Imran. He began calling them, but they did not listen to him. So he invoked against them that the rain be withheld, and they suffered a severe hardship, and Elias hid himself from them out of fear for his own life. Then he said to them one day: "You have indeed perished from hardship, and the animals and trees have perished because of your sins. Go out with your idols and call upon them; if they respond to you, then the matter is as you say, but if they do not, you will know that you are upon falsehood, and you will refrain from it, and I will call upon Allah and He will relieve you." They said: "You have been fair." So they went out with their idols and images and called upon them, but they did not respond to them, and they recognized their error and said: "Call upon Allah for us." So he called for them, and He sent the rain, and their lands came back to life, but they did not desist from what they were upon. So Elias called upon his Lord to take him to Himself and relieve him of them. It was said to him: "Go out on such a day to such a place; whatever comes to you, mount it and do not give it away." He went out, and a horse of fire approached, leapt upon him, and carried him off; Allah clothed it with feathers and dressed it in light, and cut off from it the pleasure of eating and drinking, and it flew among the angels. So he became a human angel, earthly and heavenly.

One: it gathers for this prophet and the believers in him as one people, and this is how a thing is referred to by the name of the thing; you say: "I saw the Muhallabah," meaning the sons of al-Muhallab, and "the Masami'a," meaning the sons of Masma'. 

The second: it is the name of the prophet alone, and it is a Hebrew name, and non-Arabic names are sometimes treated in this manner, as you say: Mikal and Mika'il. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj mentioned both views.

The answer: it may be a dialect form, like Ibrahim, Ibraham, and similarly the verse:

"Qadni man nasara al-Khubaybayni qadi"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 37, verse 139–148:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When he ran away﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: the interpretation of "abaqa" is that he went far away. Abu 'Ubayda said: he was alarmed. Al-Zajjaj said: he fled. Some of the people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: he went out without being permitted, and so he was like one who flees from his master. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-fulk" is the ship, "al-mashhun" is the filled, and "sahama" means "qara'a" (cast lots). ﴿Among the losers﴾, that is, among the defeated. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said, "Allah refuted (adhda'a) his argument, so it was refuted (dahadat)," that is, He removed it, so it was removed; and the origin of "al-dahd" is slipperiness.

Reference to his story

We have explained part of his story at the end of Yunus and in (al-Anbiya: 86), to the extent that the verses bear, and we mention here what they bear. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: when Yunus promised his people punishment after three days, they cried out to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and sought forgiveness, so He withheld the punishment from them. He set off in anger until he reached a people in a ship; they recognised him and carried him. When he boarded the ship, it stopped, and he said: "What is wrong with your ship?" They said: "We do not know." He said: "But I know. In it is a slave who has fled from his Lord. By Allah, it will not move until you cast him out." They said: "As for you, O Prophet of Allah, by Allah we will not cast you out." He said: "Then draw lots, and whoever is drawn, let him fall." They drew lots, and Yunus was drawn, but they refused to let him fall, so they returned to the drawing until Yunus was drawn three times. Tawus said: the captain of the ship was the one who said: "What is preventing it from moving is that among you there is an ill-omened man, so draw lots that we may cast one of us out." They drew lots, and Yunus was drawn three times.

The commentators said: Allah appointed a fish for him, and when he threw himself into the water, it swallowed him, and He commanded that it should not harm him or wound him. Then the ship set sail at that moment. The meaning of "iltaqamahu" is that it swallowed him.

﴿And he was blameworthy﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, he was sinful. It is said, "alama al-rajulu" when a man commits a sin for which he is blamed. The poet said:

[You count excuses for which there is no excuse] and whoever forsakes his brother has indeed committed blame (alama).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah﴾. There are three opinions concerning it. The first: of those who pray, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: of those who worship, said by Mujahid and Wahb ibn Munabbih. The third: the saying ﴿There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87], said by al-Hasan. 'Imran al-Qattan narrated from al-Hasan who said: "By Allah, it was nothing but a prayer he initiated in the belly of the fish." According to this view, his glorification took place in the belly of the fish. The majority of scholars hold that he meant: had it not been for what preceded for him before the fish swallowed him of glorification, ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾. Qatada said: the belly of the fish would have become a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection, but he was abundant in prayer in ease, so Allah saved him by means of that.

As for the length of his stay in the belly of the fish, there are five opinions. The first: forty days, said by Anas ibn Malik, Ka'b, Abu Malik, Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi. The second: seven days, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata'. The third: three days, said by Mujahid and Qatada. The fourth: twenty days, said by al-Dahhak. The fifth: part of a day, that it swallowed him in the forenoon and cast him out before sunset, said by al-Sha'bi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We cast him out﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, We threw him ﴿onto the barren land (bil-'ara')﴾, which is the land where nothing hides one, neither tree nor anything else; and it seems to be from the nakedness (uri) of a thing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while he was ailing (saqim)﴾, that is, sick. Ibn Mas'ud said: he was like the condition of a fledgling that has been plucked and has no feathers. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Allah revealed to the fish that it should cast him onto the land, and it cast him out with no hair on him, no skin and no nail.
